name: Müller-Thurgau

lines.s10: Müller-Thurgau is Germany's easy white: light, soft and flowery, with apple, peach and a faint whiff of nutmeg.
lines.s20: Müller-Thurgau is a German crossing, bred in 1882 to ripen early in a cool climate. It makes a light, soft white for drinking young, with apple, white peach and a gentle Muscat scent.
lines.s45: Müller-Thurgau was made on purpose. A Swiss botanist bred it in Germany in 1882, hoping for Riesling's flavour in a vine that ripens early. It grows all over Germany, and high in the Italian Alps. It tastes of apple and white peach, with a scent of elderflower and a faint note of nutmeg. It is light and soft, with mild acidity, and it is made in steel and bottled young. Pour it cold, with salads, mild cheese or a simple plate of fish. For a century its parents were thought to be Riesling and Silvaner, until DNA named a table grape, Madeleine Royale, in Silvaner's place.
lines.sale: Müller-Thurgau is the uncomplicated one: light, soft and flowery, with nothing to puzzle over. I would pour it cold at the start, with the salads and the lighter plates, for anyone who finds Riesling too sharp.

glass.lead: Apple, white peach and elderflower with a faint nutmeg note, light, soft and mild, made to be enjoyed young.

home.home: Germany, across the country, and widely in Rheinhessen, Baden and Franken. Bred at Geisenheim in 1882 by Hermann Müller, of the Swiss canton of Thurgau, it ripens early where Riesling struggles. Most is made in steel, light and soft, and sold young; dry wines are often labelled Rivaner.
home.abroad: Alto Adige and Trentino grow it high in the mountains for a fresher, more scented wine. Switzerland calls it Riesling-Silvaner, and Luxembourg and Austria call it Rivaner.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius: well chilled, as a light aromatic white.
service.glass: A white wine glass, kept small so the wine stays cold.
service.decant: No: pour it cold and young, straight from the bottle.
service.age: Enjoy it young, within a year or two of the vintage; freshness is its charm.

labels.means: The name German growers often give a dry, fresh Müller-Thurgau; also used in Luxembourg and Austria.
The Swiss name, from the parents it was long thought to have.
A mild, lightly sweet German blend in which Müller-Thurgau is one of the permitted main grapes.

guest.a: It is the breeder's name and his home: Hermann Müller, a botanist from the Swiss canton of Thurgau, bred the grape at Geisenheim in Germany in 1882.
It is a child of Riesling, but gentler: lighter, softer and lower in acidity, with a flowery, faintly Muscat scent, and meant for drinking young, not for keeping.
It can be either. Bottles labelled Rivaner or trocken are dry; others carry a little sweetness, and it is one of the grapes of soft, sweetish Liebfraumilch.

compare.tell: Riesling, its parent, has piercing acidity, lime and long life; Müller-Thurgau is softer and lighter, with a flowery nutmeg scent, and fades sooner.
Silvaner is firmer and more savoury, with pear, hay and damp earth; Müller-Thurgau is lighter and more scented, with elderflower and nutmeg.
Muscat smells loudly of fresh grapes and orange blossom; Müller-Thurgau carries only a faint Muscat note over apple and peach.

profile.st: Pale straw · Body light to medium · Acid low to medium · Alcohol low to moderate · Dry to off dry; no oak
profile.fruit: Yellow apple, ripe pear and white peach; lemon and green apple from high, cool sites; a light Muscat grape note
profile.other: Elderflower, lilac and a faint nutmeg note; fresh hay from mountain vineyards; soft, mild and made to be enjoyed young
profile.tell: Light, soft and flowery, with mild acidity and a faint nutmeg or Muscat note: Riesling's shape without its acidity or length
profile.regions: Throughout Germany, widely in Rheinhessen, Baden and Franken; Alto Adige and Trentino at altitude; Switzerland (as Riesling-Silvaner); Luxembourg and Austria (as Rivaner)
profile.confuse: Riesling has far higher acidity, lime and petrol with age; Silvaner is firmer and more savoury; Muscat is much more loudly grapey

cards.front: Müller-Thurgau: who bred it, where and when?
cards.back: Hermann Müller, a botanist from the Swiss canton of Thurgau, at Geisenheim in Germany in 1882. He wanted Riesling's character in a vine that ripens early.

cards.front: Müller-Thurgau: its true parents, and the old mistake?
cards.back: Riesling and Madeleine Royale, a table grape, as DNA work showed. For a century it was taken for Riesling crossed with Silvaner, hence Rivaner and Riesling-Silvaner.

cards.front: Müller-Thurgau in the glass: what should a taster expect?
cards.back: A pale, light, soft white with mild acidity: apple, white peach and elderflower with a faint nutmeg or Muscat note, for drinking young.

questions.q: A guest sees Rivaner on a German list and asks which grape it is. What do you answer?
questions.exp: Rivaner is a name for Müller-Thurgau, usually on a dry, fresh wine. It was coined from Riesling and Silvaner, once thought to be the parents; DNA showed Riesling and Madeleine Royale.

questions.q: A guest asks for a fresher, more scented Müller-Thurgau from high mountain vineyards. From which region do you choose it?
questions.exp: Alto Adige grows Müller-Thurgau on airy slopes up to about 1,000 metres, which keeps it fresh and scented. Rheinhessen, the Pfalz and Baden are lower and warmer.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it; a new grape, so it carries its profile and eight targets, each named in the entry: germany, rheinhessen, baden, franken, pfalz, mosel, trentino-alto-adige and switzerland.
The say line is the Codex's own respelling in its Switzerland reading, MEW-ler TOOR-gow.

The breeder is named, as the brief allows: Hermann Müller, 1882, Geisenheim, on the German wine body. One German page adds that the grape took his name in 1913; that year is left out as read once only.
The parentage, Riesling and Madeleine Royale and not Silvaner, is the Codex's own (the Régionale and Grand Cru banks) and the German wine body's.

The nutmeg note is the Alto Adige consortium's word and the light Muscat tone the German body's; lilac and geranium are the consortium's. Elderflower, nectarine and mace are tasting notes of my own beside them; a checker may strike them.

Alto Adige at altitude, 550 to 1,000 metres, stands on its consortium; Trentino on the Codex's own region record, which names the grape for Trentino-Alto Adige. Riesling-Silvaner for Switzerland is the Codex's own; Rivaner for Luxembourg and Austria stands on two glossaries.
The ladder gives Baden and the Pfalz as moderate and the rest of Germany as cool; the Codex notes Baden alone in the warmer European growing zone.
Left out: New Zealand, where the grape was once common and is now marginal, read in one source only; every figure of area or share.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
